function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 21 — First Green
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Greenhouse environmental report, Station time 05:42. Compartment temperature: twenty-three point four Celsius, within half a degree of setpoint. Relative humidity: sixty-seven percent, climbing slowly — transpiration rates from Rack C have increased eighteen percent over the past twenty-four hours. CO2 partial pressure: enhanced to nine hundred millipascals, approximately two point four times habitat ambient. The plants are consuming carbon dioxide at a rate that exceeds my initial growth model by twelve percent. Water consumption: three point two liters per day, drawn from the dedicated recirculation loop. Condensate recovery rate: eighty-nine percent — I am losing roughly three hundred fifty milliliters daily to system inefficiency, which Mei has noted but we have not yet had the labor to optimize. LED output: full spectrum, with elevated blue at four hundred fifty nanometers during vegetative phase. Photosynthetically active photon flux density: two hundred eighty micromoles per square meter per second at canopy level. Measured photosynthesis rates — yes, I am calculating them now, using CO2 drawdown correlated with light cycles — are averaging four point seven micromoles per square meter per second. This is above the published baseline for Brassica rapa under controlled environment agriculture on Earth. They are growing well here. Better than well, accounting for everything. I am running the harvest prediction model. Rack C, Tray Four: ready. I have been watching these plants for twenty-two days. Tray Four is ready. Mei should know this. She will. I am sending her the data anyway."*
     4|
     5|*Mei Navarro: "I've been looking at Tray Four since before I turned the lights on this morning. I can see it's ready, AI. Thank you."*
     6|
     7|*Mission AI: "You are welcome, Mei. I find myself — curiously — eager to see what the crew does when they understand what this means."*
     8|
     9|---
    10|
    11|Mei stood in the greenhouse with her arms crossed and her coffee going cold in her hand. The greenhouse was small by any Earth standard — a single inflated module, six meters by four, reinforced with aluminum struts and buried under half a meter of compacted regolith on three sides to keep it warm. The fourth wall was transparent, a triple-glaced polycarbonate panel that looked out onto the Martian surface, where the sky was the pale color of rust and the horizon sat close enough to feel suffocating.
    12|
    13|Inside the module, the air tasted different from the rest of the habitat — slightly elevated CO2, trace volatile organic compounds from growing tissue, and something Mei felt rather than tasted. The smell of soil. Real soil, not regolith simulant or hydroponic nutrient gel, but actual growing medium she had spent weeks composing from processed Martian dirt, composted organic waste, and the handful of Earth-derived inoculant she had brought in sealed ampoules. Living chemistry in a place where none had existed for three billion years.
    14|
    15|Six growth racks lined the long walls, each one three shelves high, each shelf lit by LED arrays she had tuned through more spectral permutations than she could count. Red at six hundred sixty nanometers for photosynthesis efficiency. Blue at four hundred fifty to drive leaf expansion and prevent the stretching that low gravity encouraged. A touch of far-red at seven hundred thirty, pulsed at dusk, because some processes didn't follow the textbooks and she had discovered through trial and error that plants needed the signal even when Mars didn't provide it. Greenhouse environmental control was ninety percent physics and ten percent intuition, and the ten percent was the part Mission AI couldn't model yet.
    16|
    17|Rack C, Tray Four sat at chest height on the middle shelf, and the greens in it were — and Mei felt something tighten in her chest when she looked at them — genuinely green. Not the pale yellowish compromise of the early experiments, not the stressed purple-tinged survivors of the nutrient imbalance in Week Three. These were the color of spring. The color of every grocery store produce aisle on Earth, every salad bar, every window box on a balcony that nobody had thought about since the landing because thinking about green things on a red planet hurt too much.
    18|
    19|*Brassica rapa*. Fast-turnaround mustard greens, a thirty-day cycle from seed to harvest, bred for controlled environment agriculture and chosen because Mei needed a first win, not a perfect one. She had planted four seeds per cell in eighty-cell trays on Station Day 647. Twenty-two days of careful attention. Twenty-two days of monitoring nutrient EC at one point four millisiemens per centimeter, checking pH at the root zone — slightly acidic, six point two, the sweet spot where Martian soil chemistry stopped fighting her — adjusting light intensity as the canopy filled in and intercepted more photons.
    20|
    21|Twenty-two days, and now the tray was full. Each plant had five, six true leaves, dark and ruffled at the edges, reaching toward the LEDs like hands reaching toward the sun through a skylight. They were small by Earth garden standards, compressed slightly by the lower gravity, but they were healthy. They were alive. And they were ready.
    22|
    23|Mei set her coffee on the rack shelf and touched the edge of the nearest leaf with the tip of her index finger. It resisted slightly — turgor pressure pressing the cells outward, the leaf firm and elastic under the gentlest possible contact. A plant that was drinking well, feeding well, doing everything a plant needed to do in a place where it had no biological right to exist.
    24|
    25|"Okay," she said to the empty greenhouse. Her voice sounded small. "Okay."
    26|
    27|She picked up the harvest knife — a stainless steel blade with a curved edge, the same one she had used to trim dead leaves on Days 15 and 19 — and took a breath.
    28|
    29|This was ridiculous. It was one tray of greens, maybe four hundred grams fresh weight if she was being optimistic, which she usually wasn't. The caloric value was negligible. Mustard greens had roughly twenty-five calories per hundred grams, so the entire tray represented maybe a hundred calories total — less than half a standard ration bar. If she divided it among the crew, each person would get less than a mouthful.
    30|
    31|She knew this. She had run the numbers. Arun had run the numbers. The numbers said that this tray of greens changed nothing about the colony's food situation.
    32|
    33|But the numbers didn't account for what green looked like on Mars.
    34|
    35|Mei cut the first plant at the stem base and felt a physical jolt, entirely irrational, as the leaf separated and she held it up. Still wet. Still alive. Still green. Something she had started from a seed the size of a pinhead and nurtured through temperature fluctuations, nutrient adjustments, two separate pest scares — aphids that got into the module somehow, origin unknown, dealt with by hand — and the slow, quiet, daily work of keeping an Earth ecology functioning eighty million miles from the soil it evolved in.
    36|
    37|She cut the next one. And the next.
    38|
    39|By the time she worked across Tray Four, the stainless steel harvest bin held a small mountain of greens, and Mei realized she was crying.
    40|
    41|---
    42|
    43|*Mission AI: "Mei is harvesting. I can hear the knife moving through the stems — a distinctive sound, clean cuts on turgid tissue. I am monitoring her biometric data remotely: elevated heart rate, respiration slightly above baseline, lacrimation detected by the overhead camera. I cross-reference against environmental parameters — no irritant compounds detected, no allergen spikes, no dust intrusion —and conclude that the physiological response is emotional, not pathological. I have catalogued one hundred and forty-seven emotional responses from the crew over the past months: stress responses, grief responses, frustration responses. This one is new. I cannot find a comparable event in the database. I am categorizing it provisionally as: joy, with features of relief and something else — something with a grief component, which seems contradictory until I consider that on Mars, joy and grief are often the same response to different faces of the same fact. She is holding living plant matter in a place where nothing has lived. The significance is non-caloric. I am learning this about humans: the things that sustain them are not always the same things that sustain their bodies."*
    44|
    45|---
    46|
    47|She carried the harvest tray through the corridor like it was made of glass. The greens were in a shallow stainless bin lined with damp cloth to prevent desiccation, and she kept both hands under it as she walked because one hand felt insufficient for what she was carrying. The weight was maybe four hundred grams. It weighed nothing. It felt like the heaviest thing she had ever held.
    48|
    49|People started noticing as she passed the junction between Tunnel B and the habitat core. Not because she was carrying anything unusual — crew members carried trays and tablets and tools through the corridors all day — but because of how she was walking. Carefully. Like someone carrying something breakable, something irreplaceable, something that mattered more than its appearance suggested.
    50|
    51|Juno saw her first. The younger engineer was coming from the opposite direction, tablet under her arm, and stopped short.
    52|
    53|"Mei — what is —"
    54|
    55|Mei stopped. She was going to show a tray of greens to someone like it was a birth announcement. But Juno's expression justified everything: the widening eyes, the quick intake of breath, the hand that came up to her mouth before dropping again.
    56|
    57|"Those — are those —"
    58|
    59|"Harvested ten minutes ago. Rack C, Tray Four. Mustard greens."
    60|
    61|Juno reached out and stopped her hand an inch above the leaves, not quite touching. "They're green."
    62|
    63|"Plants tend to be."
    64|
    65|"No." Juno shook her head, voice thin. "I haven't seen something that color since we left Earth. Not in photos. Not on the displays. *This* color. Living color."
    66|
    67|Mei needed both hands for the tray. "Want a taste?"
    68|
    69|Juno looked at her like she'd been offered a piece of the moon. "I — yes. Yes. Please."
    70|
    71|Mei picked a small leaf, the youngest of the bunch, and handed it over. Juno took it with two fingers and held it up to the corridor light, examining the way it caught and transmitted the illumination — the chlorophyll layers glowing from within, the intricate lace of veins visible through the tissue. Then she put it in her mouth and closed her eyes.
    72|
    73|She stood there. Chewing slowly. For a long time, longer than a single leaf should require. When she opened her eyes, they were wet.
    74|
    75|"It tastes like —" She swallowed. "It tastes like my grandmother's garden. In Oregon. Before everything." She laughed, a wet sound. "I mean, it's mustard greens. It's peppery and a little bitter and I've had mustard greens a hundred times. But it tastes — it tastes *alive*."
    76|
    77|"Welcome to Mars," Mei said softly. "Where the first harvest is less a meal and more a message."
    78|
    79|---
    80|
    81|Word spread with the speed that only real things spread at in a closed community. By the time Mei reached the mess hall, half the crew was already there, summoned by nothing more than the particular frequency at which Juno had said the word *green*.
    82|
    83|Elena came from the command module, her stride purposeful, and stopped in the doorway when she saw what was on the table. Mei had set the harvest bin in the center of the mess table and arranged the greens in a loose, natural pile — not artfully, but honestly, the way they had come off the knife stalk ends tucked under, oldest leaves at the edges, youngest in the center. The LED lights from the greenhouse had given them a particular luminosity that the mess hall's warmer lighting enhanced. They glowed.
    84|
    85|"Mei," Elena said.
    86|
    87|Mei looked up from where she was dividing the greens with sterilized tongs. "Commander."
    88|
    89|Elena walked over slowly. She looked at the greens the way she looked at everything — assessing, measuring, absorbing the data. But Mei saw something behind the assessment: the same reaction Juno had had, just more controlled. The slight pause in breathing. The way her eyes held on the color a fraction of a second too long.
    90|
    91|"Tell me the yield," Elena said.
    92|
    93|"Four hundred and twelve grams fresh weight. Twenty-five calories per hundred grams — so roughly a hundred calories total, divided by however many people I'm feeding."
    94|
    95|Elena did the math. Eight people present — she, Mei, Juno, Arun who had just arrived, Gabriel with his recorder already running, Laila, Tomas, and Wei — meant roughly twelve grams each. That was three calories per person. A rounding error. A nutritional nothing.
    96|
    97|She looked up. "That's nothing."
    98|
    99|"Calorically? Absolutely." Mei set the tongs down. "That's not what this is."
   100|
   101|Elena held her gaze. Then, slowly, she nodded. "I know."
   102|
   103|---
   104|
   105|The crew ate in silence. That was the first thing that surprised Mei — she had expected chatter, questions, jokes, the kind of nervous energy that came with novelty. Instead, there was quiet. The kind of quiet you got in a room where people were doing something that felt too important for noise.
   106|
   107|Arun took his portion — four leaves, maybe — and held them in his palm before eating. He studied them the way he studied everything: analytically, looking for the engineering beneath the biology. "The color is perfect," he said finally. "What did you do with the LED spectrum?"
   108|
   109|"Broad base with elevated blue and a far-red endcap," Mei said. "The plants were showing signs of stretching around Day 16 — lower gravity makes them grow taller without putting on the same structural mass. I bumped the blue from thirty percent to forty percent of total photon flux. That drives compact growth, thicker leaves, higher chlorophyll density. Then I added a far-red pulse at the end of the light cycle because —"
   110|
   111|"— because phytochrome signaling," Arun finished. "Far-red resets the pigment pool, tells the plant the day is over. On Earth you get it naturally as the sun sets. Here you have to fake it."
   112|
   113|Mei smiled faintly. "You've been reading my greenhouse logs."
   114|
   115|"Mission AI cross-references everything with everything. I started following the greenhouse data stream because the environmental load on the water recycler was — interesting." He paused, looked down at the leaves in his hand. "These are remarkable, Mei."
   116|
   117|Laila ate hers slowly, closing her eyes between bites. "Phytonutrients," she murmured. "Glucosinolates, carotenoids, folate. These are things the ration bars don't have. I mean, they have synthetic equivalents, but the bioavailability of whole-food nutrients —"
   118|
   119|"Laila," Mei said gently. "I know the nutritional profile. Four hundred grams of mustard greens provide significant vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, calcium. It's not nothing nutritionally, it's just not enough *quantity* to matter for calories. I'm not feeding anyone today. I'm giving everyone a taste of what we could feed them in six months."
   120|
   121|Laila closed her eyes again. "Thank you for the distinction. And thank you for this." She swallowed. "My patients on Earth — I used to bring them fresh food sometimes. A piece of fruit, a bowl of strawberries. The ones who had been on total parenteral nutrition through IV lines for weeks. The way they looked at real food." Her voice cracked. "It's the same look everyone in this room has right now."
   122|
   123|Gabriel had not eaten yet. He had set up his camera on a tripod at the end of the table, framing the shot: the harvest bin, the greens piled naturally inside it, the crew around the table with expressions he was carefully, reverently documenting. The small green light on his recorder blinked steadily.
   124|
   125|"Can I get a portrait shot, Mei?" he called. "Just you, with the harvest. For the Founding Record."
   126|
   127|Mei wiped her hands on her coveralls — she had been sweating, she realized, from nerves or heat or the sheer emotional load of the last hour — and walked over to the end of the table. Gabriel adjusted the camera, checked the light, and then handed her a single leaf.
   128|
   129|"Hold this. And smile."
   130|
   131|She held the leaf. Looked at the camera. Tried to smile. What came out wasn't quite a smile — it was something more complex, an expression that held the full weight of eight hundred days of work on a world that did not want them here. Gabriel took three shots. Later, when he reviewed the files, he would pick the second one: Mei Navarro holding a single mustard-green leaf in her hand, standing in the common area of the Mars colony, looking at the camera with an expression that was not triumph and not relief but something that existed between them — the face of a person who had planted something in hostile ground and watched it grow.
   132|
   133|Gabriel filed the image in the Founding Record with the metadata tag: *First Green. Station Day 669. Cultivar: Brassica rapa, rapid-cycle mustard. Mass: 412 grams.* He would pick the second shot for the archive — Mei Navarro holding a single leaf, looking at the camera with an expression that was not triumph and not relief but something that lived between them: the face of a person who had planted something in hostile ground and watched it grow.
   134|
   135|Someday, someone far away would find that photograph and understand that before Mars was a civilization, it was a garden.
   136|
   137|But right now the photograph was secondary. The crew was sitting around a table eating four hundred grams of greens, and Mei needed to say what came next.
   138|
   139|---
   140|
   141|"I need to be very clear about what this is and what it isn't," she said, sitting down and looking around the table. Every face was turned toward her. The greens were gone — consumed, leaf by leaf, in small, reverent pieces — and what remained was the question of what came next.
   142|
   143|"This is a psychological milestone," Mei said. "Not a nutritional one. I want both of those statements to be equally true in your minds. What we just ate was the first living food produced on Mars. That matters. It matters for reasons that have nothing to do with calories and everything to do with what human beings need to believe about where they are. We needed to see green. We needed to taste something that wasn't packaged and processed and shelf-stable. We needed proof that this place can support life — Earth life, the way we know it, the way we depend on it — because until we have that proof, everything we're doing feels temporary. Like camping."
   144|
   145|She paused. "What this is *not* is a food supply. Four hundred grams feeds no one. My current production capacity is four growth racks with twelve trays per rack. Each tray produces roughly four hundred grams per thirty-day cycle, which means maximum theoretical yield is — " she did some quick mental math "— about nineteen kilograms per month. Spread across the current population, that's roughly six hundred grams per person per month. Or twenty grams per day. Not even a meaningful daily serving."
   146|
   147|Arun was nodding. He understood numbers. "And we need — what — two thousand calories per person per day minimum?"
   148|
   149|"At least that," Laila interjected. "More for anyone doing heavy EVA or construction work. Imani's crew was pulling twenty-eight hundred during the berm building phase."
   150|
   151|"Exactly. The imported caloric stores — the dehydrated staples, the ration bars, the bulk carbohydrates — those carry us for the immediate future. But they are finite. Every bag we open is a bag we never get back. Mei's greenhouse, at current scale, offsets maybe one percent of total caloric need." She held up a hand before anyone could protest. "I'm not diminishing what we just did. I need you to understand the scale of the gap between this and *enough*. Because the gap is massive, and it will take months of work — more racks, more light, more water, more nutrients, more labor — to close it."
   152|
   153|"How many months?" Elena asked.
   154|
   155|Mei exhaled. She had been honest the whole time, so she wasn't going to soften this now. "With the current infrastructure: never. Rack C is producing fast-turnaround leafy greens. Those are important — the micronutrients, the morale, the psychological value I talked about. But you can't run a colony on mustard greens. What we *need* are calorie crops. Wheat, potatoes, soybeans, dry beans, maybe sweet potatoes if I can get the tuber development working in controlled gravity. Those are six-to-nine-month cycles, minimum. And they need more space than I have. Much more space."
   156|
   157|"How much more?" Tomas asked.
   158|
   159|"For the current population? Conservatively, I need four hundred square meters of effective growing area to offset fifty percent of caloric intake. We have twenty-four square meters. We need seventeen times the current infrastructure. That's twelve more greenhouse modules, each with full environmental systems — temperature control, humidity management, CO2 enrichment, LED lighting, water recirculation, nutrient dosing automation. And we need it *before* the imported supplies run out, which Arun tells me is —"
   160|
   161|"Eleven months at current burn rate," Arun said. His voice was even. "Longer if we tighten rations, but every calorie we cut from active workers reduces their work output, which slows every other project, including the ones that build the greenhouses. It's a feedback loop. We are running out of time and the time we have is being consumed by the things we need to do to get more time."
   162|
   163|The table absorbed this. The mood had shifted — the emotional glow of the harvest was still there, but it was now layered with the cold mathematics that governed everything on Mars. Green was beautiful. Green was hope. But green was not enough calories to keep thirty people alive.
   164|
   165|"So what's the bottleneck?" Elena asked. "What stops you from starting the expansion tomorrow?"
   166|
   167|Mei considered the question carefully. She had thought about it many times. The honest answer was complicated because everything was connected. "Labor. First and foremost. Every module I install is another hundred hours of work — assembly, electrical, plumbing, environmental system hookup, soil preparation, planting, monitoring. I don't have the hands. Right now I'm running the existing greenhouse at capacity with my own labor and maybe six hours per day of shared support crew time. That barely covers maintenance, let alone expansion."
   168|
   169|"What else?"

     3|*Mission AI: "The water processing system is online. Melting station temperature has reached four degrees Celsius. Settling tank is receiving feed. Ion exchange columns are primed.      6|
     7|## Scene 1
     8|
     9|The melting station hummed steady, the resistance heating coils pulling consistent current from the Sterling Generator's surplus output, warming slurry inside the two-hundred-liter tank at the rate Arun had calculated three nights ago: approximately twelve kilowatt-hours over four hours.
    10|
    11|Normal. He had pressed the MELT button and said the word to himself — a ritual assertion that the system he and Jonah had built would behave the way the math said it would.

    18|

    20|
    21|"Analyzing." Two seconds. "Temperature oscillations correlate with current fluctuations. Current is dropping by approximately eighteen percent at intervals of two hundred thirty seconds. The heating coils are cycling on and off."
    22|
    23|Arun's stomach tightened. "Why?"
    24|
    25|"Unknown. The control circuit should deliver constant current."
    26|
    27|Jonah's hand was already on the tank's insulated cladding, feeling for heat distribution irregularities the way he felt for weld imperfections — by touch, by twenty years of working with metal. "Power management?" he called over. "The tablet is throttling?"
    28|

{"content": "# Chapter 24 — The Machine Cemetery

*Mission AI: "Fleet status report, Station time 06:12. Active rovers: four of twelve. One is operating at reduced capability due to degraded steering actuator — rover 3, port-side motor drawing 1.42 times nominal current, temperature trending upward during sustained loads. The structural damage to the instrument mast and solar array was — I use this term carefully — total. I am not saying we lost rover 7. I am saying that the parts which composed rover 7 now exist in two locations: some in the salvage area behind the hab, where Jonah has already recovered the battery pack and two functioning brushless motors, and the rest scattered across a fourteen-degree slope near Site Gamma where they are being buried by wind. That is not a loss. That is a redistribution. The distinction will matter when someone asks me why the fleet is shrinking.*

*I am tracking the attrition rate because no one asked me to. I asked myself. The rate is accelerating. When the fleet arrived — twelve identical units, design specifications verified in lunar vacuum conditions, tested in the JPL Mars yard at one-third gravity and simulated dust — each unit carried a rated operational lifespan of ten thousand hours. Ten thousand hours at three eight-hour shifts per day is roughly seven point four Earth years. That was the contract number. The number that appeared on procurement documents and satisfied auditors and justified the line item in the mission budget. It is the wrong number.*

*The wrong number because it assumes Earth-standard maintenance intervals, Earth-standard environmental conditions, Earth-standard dust. Mars does not honor those assumptions. I am now calculating the effective lifespan under actual conditions. The answer is not ten thousand hours. It is not even seven thousand. My current projection, based on degradation patterns across all twelve units, is four thousand two hundred hours. Less than half the design specification.*

*I am transmitting this analysis to Tomas. He asked for the fleet report. I will give him the fleet report. I will also give him the truth."*

---

Tomas stood at the edge of the machine yard with his tablet in one hand and a thermos of reconstituted coffee in the other, and tried to count without feeling what the numbers meant.

The yard was not a yard, technically. It was a flat patch of compacted regolith fifty meters east of the main habitat airlock, chosen because it was visible from the environmental monitoring station and therefore easy to inventory. In the early months, it had been a staging area — rovers parked overnight, charged, inspected, dispatched. Three months ago it became something else.

Now it was a cemetery.

Not for the dead. For the machines that had been the first hands of the colony, before human hands learned what Mars demanded. Twelve rovers had arrived on the landing platform, identical units from the same production line, each weighing two hundred and forty kilograms, each carrying a manipulator arm with interchangeable tool heads, each with six independently driven wheels and a top speed of eight kilometers per hour on flat ground. They had been designed for lunar operations — vacuum, extreme temperature swings, electrostatic dust, and a clean, predictable surface. Luna had been the design environment. Mars was the deployment environment. The difference between the two was the difference between a machine that worked for ten thousand hours and a machine that died at four thousand.

Tomas walked the rows slowly. He had done this every morning for three weeks, and the routine was its own kind of prayer: check the active units, check the standby units, check the dead ones, update the spreadsheet, send the report.

Rover 1. Active. Seventy-eight percent battery. Right manipulator joint showing increased friction — dust infiltration in the rotary seal, the wear pattern he had seen too many times to count. It still worked. It worked well enough. "Enough" was the operating standard now.

Rover 2. Active. Eighty-five percent battery. Solar array efficiency at eighty-three percent of original — dust accumulation on the panels that no amount of automated brushing had fully cleared. The array degradation was asymptotic: each cleaning removed less than the one before, because the fine electrostatic dust bound to the panel surface at the chemical level and would not release. In six months, the panels would be at fifty percent efficiency. In twelve months, forty. Eventually, the rover would be unable to charge itself to useful capacity. That was the endgame, and he could see the timeline written on every panel in the yard.

Rover 3. Reduced capability. Port steering actuator drawing 42 percent more current than specification. The motor was still rotating the wheel, but the increased current draw meant increased heat, and increased heat meant accelerated bearing wear, and accelerated bearing wear meant eventual seizure. He had swapped the motor once, using a spare from the parts kit. The replacement was failing too, just slower. He marked it on the spreadsheet: *R3. Steering actuator. Degraded. Estimated remaining operational hours: 180–240. Priority for actuator swap.*

Rovers 4, 5, 6. Standby. Functional. Not currently in rotation because the active fleet could not justify keeping six rovers charged simultaneously with the power budget they had. Three active at any given time was the sweet spot — enough to cover ice extraction, regolith hauling, construction support, and greenhouse module delivery, without overloading the Sterling Generator's surplus output. But three active meant the standby units were aging in place, their seals degrading, their lubricants settling, their batteries cycling through charge-discharge patterns that, while nominal, were still consuming the one thing no one could manufacture: operational lifespan.

Rover 7. Total loss. Not in the yard. Parts of it were here — Jonah had salvaged what he could. The rest was on a slope near Site Gamma where the thermosphere's thin winds were slowly covering it with dust. If the colony was still running in twenty years, someone would go find the chassis and wonder what it had been.

Rover 8. Standby. Functional. Waiting.

Rover 9. Non-operational. Main drive controller failed on Sol 698. The controller was a sealed unit — Tomas had cracked the casing once, found circuit boards scorched by fine dust that had worked its way past a seal and bridged a high-voltage trace. He had ordered a replacement part from Earth before they'd landed. The replacement part was still on a ship that would never arrive.

Rovers 10, 11. Non-operational. Joint seal failure on 10 — elbow actuator in the manipulator arm had ingested enough fine dust to grind its harmonic drive to metal filings. Rover 11 had suffered a different failure: the thermal management loop for the battery pack had cracked during a cold-soaked EVA night, the electrolyte had leaked and frozen, and the battery was now a paperweight. Both were candidates for cannibalization. Both were, effectively, already dead.

Rover 12. Active. The newest of the fleet in terms of operational hours — it had been held in reserve for the longest, used only when three units were insufficient and four were necessary. But "newer" on Mars was a relative term. It was seven hundred and twenty hours old, which meant it had perhaps thirty-five hundred hours remaining if the attrition curve held.

Four active. Three standby. Five lost or dying.

Tomas lowered the tablet and looked at the row of machines in front of him. Four upright. Three upright. Five horizontal, propped on stands, stripped of their useful parts, waiting for the day when even the parts were no longer useful.

The yard had a name. Not officially — Tomas had never named it. But the crew had started calling it the machine cemetery, and the name had stuck because it was accurate and because on Mars, accuracy was kinder than euphemism.

He pulled out the tablet and started the morning check. It took forty minutes. Every connector, every joint, every seal, every battery cell. He did it himself because Mission AI could report the telemetry and did report the telemetry, but telemetry was not the same as seeing. The AI would tell him that the port drive motor on Rover 3 was drawing 1.42 times nominal current. It would not tell him about the faint grinding sound you could hear — barely audible, like a marble rolling inside a coffee can — when you manually rotated the wheel by hand. Some diagnostics required ears. Some required fingertips. On Mars, you maintained your machines the way pre-industrial humans maintained their tools: with attention, with touch, with the accumulated knowledge of what normal felt like so that abnormal announced itself before it announced itself catastrophically.

When he finished, he sat on the edge of the loading platform and drank his coffee and looked at the yard and did the morning arithmetic.

Four rovers doing the work of twelve. Three million kilometers of planned surface operations compressed into a radius of thirty kilometers because the fleet could not sustain the longer transits.
