The math was not catastrophic. Not yet. It was insidious. It was the math of a resource that was being consumed faster than it could be replaced, where the replacement rate was zero. Every hour a rover spent operating was an hour subtracted from a finite total. Every EVA accelerated the timeline. Every dust storm advanced it. Every time a rover returned to the yard with fine red dust worked into its joints and seals and circuit board edges, the countdown moved forward by an amount that could not be measured precisely but could be felt with increasing certainty.

Mission AI sent the morning fleet report to his tablet. Tomas read it while the coffee cooled. The AI's analysis matched his own — the attrition rate was tracking slightly worse than his projections, not better. The difference was small: maybe two hundred hours across the fleet. But small differences compounded. Small differences were how systems failed.

He closed the tablet. The yard was silent except for the faint wind that always blew on Mars and the distant hum of the life support systems. Four upright. Five down. Three standing by, getting older every day they stood still.

The cemetery was growing. After every EVA, it grew a little more.

---

The briefing room was too small for what it had to contain. Thirty people in a space designed for twelve, standing where they could find room, sitting on equipment cases when the walls ran out. Elena took the center position near the display table, and the quiet that fell was the particular quality of quiet that meant the room knew something important was coming.

Tomas stood beside the table with his tablet projected onto the wall screen. The graph he had built was simple by design: a line tracking total fleet operational hours against time, with two reference lines — the manufacturer's design specification at ten thousand hours, and the actual attrition curve based on real Mars data, plotted from their own operational logs.

The two lines diverged like roads heading to different continents.

"Let me start with the design specification," Tomas said. His voice was flat, professional. The kind of voice you used when the numbers were bad and the only thing worse than bad numbers was emotional delivery of bad numbers. "Each rover in our fleet was designed for ten thousand operational hours. That's the figure on the spec sheet. Ten thousand hours at nominal conditions — lunar vacuum, controlled dust environment, manufacturer-recommended maintenance intervals. It was a good number. It was the right number for the environment the machines were designed for."

He tapped the screen. The second line appeared, lower, steeper, heading toward zero much faster than the first. "This is what we're actually getting. Four thousand two hundred hours, current projection. Less than half the design specification. And this number is not stable — it could easily come down further as the fleet ages and the degradation curves accelerate."

A murmur moved through the room. Not panic. Calculation. People running the math in their heads, connecting Tomas's numbers to their own work, understanding what a sixty percent reduction meant.

"Why?" It was Elena. Not because she didn't understand the why — she had read the preliminary reports — but because she wanted it said aloud for everyone.

"Three primary failure modes." Tomas pulled up the analysis: a tri-fold chart, each quadrant a different failure mechanism, each annotated with data. "First and worst: dust infiltration. Martian dust is not like lunar dust. It's finer, it's electrostatically charged, and it's chemically reactive. Perchlorates on the grain surfaces create a corrosive environment inside the joints. Every seal on every actuator is designed for clean vacuum. Mars gives it dust. The dust works past the seals. It gets into the bearings, the gears, the motor windings, the circuit board conformal coating. Once it's in, it doesn't come out. I can't clean it out. The manufacturer's recommended cleaning protocol — compressed gas blowdown and ultrasonic bath — those assume Earth-side maintenance facilities with proper equipment. We have a shop and what Jonah can fabricate. That's not nothing, but it's not enough."

He swiped to the second quadrant. "Second: seal degradation. The rotary and linear seals on the joint actuators are made from fluoroelastomer — good stuff in vacuum, rated for extreme temperature cycling. But Martian temperatures cycle differently than lunar temperatures. The atmosphere — thin as it is — changes the heat transfer profile. Cold-soak on the exterior of a seal while the interior stays warm creates shear stress the material wasn't designed for. I'm seeing micro-cracking on seals that are less than a third of their rated cycle life. And once a seal cracks, dust comes in faster. It's a feedback loop. Worse seal, more dust, more wear, worse seal."

Swiped again. Third quadrant. "Third: thermal management. The rovers use a passive heat rejection system — radiator panels that depend on infrared emission to space. On the Moon, that works. There is no atmosphere to convect heat back to the surface. On Mars, there is an atmosphere. Thin, yes. But during the day, the ambient temperature can reach minus twenty Celsius. The radiators reject heat, then the atmosphere puts some of it back. The net result is that the rovers run hotter than designed on the sunny side and colder than designed on the dark side. The temperature swings are wider than the manufacturer's thermal spec, and the thermal expansion-contraction cycles are fatiguing materials that were never meant to flex this much."

He paused. The room was absorbing it.

"So," Arun said, filling the silence with the question everyone was asking without words. "Ten thousand hours design life becomes four thousand in practice. What does that mean in terms of fleet availability?"

"It means that at our current operational tempo — which is three rovers active per day, averaging six hours of surface time each — we are consuming approximately eighteen rover-hours per day. At the current fleet average of roughly fifteen hundred hours remaining per surviving unit, we have approximately five active units and three standby units. The five active units carry a combined remaining lifespan of roughly — " Tomas did the math on the calculator rather than mentally; he had learned to trust the calculator for numbers that mattered "— six thousand three hundred hours. Divided by eighteen per day is three hundred and fifty days."

He looked up. "Eleven and a half months. That's the fleet life at current utilization if the attrition rate stays constant. It won't. It will accelerate as the machines age and the degradation curves go nonlinear. The realistic number is eight to ten months before we are down to one or two functioning rovers."

Another silence. Heavier this time. Because eight to ten months was a number everyone could map onto projects: the greenhouse expansion that needed rover-delivered materials. The ice extraction runs that fed the water production lines. The regolith block manufacturing for the secondary habitat. The solar array maintenance. The perimeter reconnaissance. The construction of the airlock corridor between Ship Two and the secondary hab.

All of it depended on machines. And the machines were dying.

"What happens when we lose them?" Elena asked. Not rhetorically. She needed the answer.

"We replace them with human labor," Tomas said. "That's the answer, and it's the one I don't want to give. Without rovers, every surface operation becomes an EVA. Every EVA requires suited personnel, which means pulling people from their primary duties. Imani's ice convoys — those were rover-driven, one or two operators per convoy. Without rovers, you need suited workers to manually haul ice. Two hundred kilograms of ice per trip weighs — " he paused "— approximately two hundred kilograms on Mars. That's three humans in suits carrying loads on uneven terrain. In conditions where suit failure is the consequence of a misstep. The colony cannot survive on manual labor for things the machines were meant to do."

"How many person-hours per EVA day?" Arun asked.

"Conservatively? Eight hours of suited labor per person, for every operation the rovers currently perform. Ice extraction, regolith movement, construction support, equipment transport, solar array dusting. Right now it takes three rovers and maybe four people — two operators and two standby. Without rovers, it takes — I'm estimating — sixteen people in suits, across two shifts, and the fatigue factor means the second shift is twenty percent less effective than the first." Tomas looked around the room. "We are thirty people. Sixteen in suits means over half the colony is doing rover work. Nothing else gets done."

Jonah, standing near the back with his arms crossed, spoke up. His voice was quiet, the voice of a man who had already been thinking about this problem in a different register — not in hours and people but in metal and parts and the practical geometry of salvage.

"We cannibalize," he said.

The room shifted toward him.

"We cannibalize the worst units," Jonah continued. "Rover 9, the drive controller is dead but the motors, the arms, the wheels — all good. Rover 10, the elbow actuator is ground to nothing but the base joint, the tool head, the battery — those are fine. Rover 12 is relatively low-hours. We strip the dead ones for parts. The parts that are still good. And we use them to extend the lives of the ones that are still running. We buy ourselves time."

Tomas nodded slowly. He had expected this. He had already thought about it. "It's a short-term strategy. Every time we cannibalize a unit, the total number of available machines goes down. Yes, we get more hours from the survivors — maybe an extra five hundred hours per unit if we swap in healthy motors, fresh controllers, clean seals. But we also reduce our fleet's redundancy. Right now, if one rover breaks down during an EVA, we have three others to cover its functions. If we strip one to save the others and we're down to three active units, a breakdown during a critical operation means the operation stops until we fix the broken unit or substitute human labor — which is the scenario I just described."

"We do it anyway," Jonah said. "Because short-term time is the only time we have."

Tomas considered this. He had been a robotics engineer for twenty years and he had never built a machine without assuming that replacement parts would eventually arrive from a supply chain. The supply chain had been the invisible foundation beneath every machine design in human history: manufacture it, deploy it, maintain it, replace it. The Mars colony had no replacement parts. The machines that existed were the machines that would ever exist. Unless someone built new ones.

"I can make it work," Tomas said. "Jonah is right. We cannibalize. I'll prioritize the parts recovery — motors, controllers, seals, battery cells, solar panels. We'll rebuild the worst units with the best parts from the others. We'll lose three rovers to save five. But —" He held up a finger. "When I'm done, we'll have five rovers instead of four active, and a fleet that can maybe last twelve months instead of eight. That's four extra months. That's something. But it's not enough."

Elena absorbed the numbers. The room absorbed them. Eleven months became eight, became four, became twelve with cannibalization. It wasn't a solution. It was a postponement.

---

The salvage work started that afternoon because on Mars, when a problem was identified, the time between identification and first action was measured in minutes, not days.

Jonah set up the work area in the fabrication bay — the same space where he had built heat exchangers, insulation retrofits, water processing retrofits, and half the improvised hardware that kept the colony breathing. The bay smelled of ozone and hot metal and the particular sharp scent of cutting fluid that never fully went away no matter how much filtration you ran. It also smelled of Mars dust now — the faint iron-oxide tang that had worked its way into every surface and would never leave, the smell of the planet itself seeping into human space.

Rover 9 was the first victim. It sat on the work platform, its six wheels still, its manipulator arm drooping, the main drive controller — a sealed aluminum housing bolted to the chassis — dead and irrecoverable. Jonah approached it the way a surgeon might approach a patient he knew he couldn't save but whose parts might save someone else.

"Mission AI, log the teardown of Rover 9, Sol 718. Beginning with the drive controller housing removal."

*Acknowledged. Recording.*

Jonah started with the bolts — M6 titanium, corroded at the threads where Martian humidity (yes, there was humidity, microscopic) had reacted with the metal over months of service. He used a solvent to penetrate the threads, waited twenty minutes, applied torque with a calibrated wrench. One by one, the bolts came free. The housing lifted off, revealing a circuit board inside that was coated in a fine layer of red dust.

"Here's your failure," Jonah said, and pointed at the board. "Dust on the high-voltage traces. You can see it — the bridging between traces 14 and 16. It shorted, took the controller with it. Tomas — is this recoverable?"

Tomas leaned in, examining the board under the bay's magnifying lamp. "No. The traces are fused. Even if I desolder the damaged sections and bridge with wire — the controller uses a custom ASIC that I can't source. It would require a full board replacement, and I don't have a board."

"Strip it for connectors and wire," Jonah said. It was the logic of salvage: everything had value, even the dead things. "The connectors are standard. We can reuse them on the surviving units. And the wire — there is maybe four meters of shielded high-current cable in this housing, and I'll bet Tomas needs it."

Tomas nodded. "I do. Always."

They worked for three hours on Rover 9. The manipulator arm came next — Jonah unbolted the shoulder joint, the elbow pivot, the wrist rotation, laying each component on the work bay in neat rows. Each component was inspected: shoulder joint, bearing smooth, minor dust ingress at the seal interface — cleanable with solvent and compressed gas. Elbow pivot, harmonic drive damaged — the gear teeth were ground smooth from dust contamination, the entire unit scrap. Wrist rotation, functional but seal degraded — resealable with a new O-ring if Jonah could machine one to spec.

"Mission AI," Tomas said during the teardown. "Cross-reference the salvaged components against the active fleet's needs."

*Processing. Shoulder joint from Rover 9 is compatible with Rovers 1, 4, and 5 — all show elevated bearing wear in the shoulder axis. Wrist rotation unit from Rover 9, pending reseal, is compatible with Rovers 2 and 3. Solar array panels from Rover 9 are degraded to sixty-two percent efficiency, below the threshold for effective re-deployment. Battery pack is functional — eighty-one percent of original capacity — and is directly compatible with all active units.*

"Strip the battery," Tomas said. "Reallocate it to Rover 3 — the one with the failing steering actuator. The extra capacity won't fix the actuator, but it will give us more margin on the power budget, which means the overheating steering motor has a little more headroom before it triggers a thermal shutdown."

*Logged. I should note: the battery pack transfer requires removal of Rover 9's main bus wiring harness, which is a thirty-minute procedure, and re-termination at the Rover 3 bus. I estimate the net time investment is forty-five minutes for a capacity increase of approximately eighteen percent on Rover 3. In terms of operational hours gained, this translates to approximately forty additional surface hours before Rover 3's battery becomes the limiting factor.*

"Forty hours is worth forty-five minutes," Tomas said.

*It would be less efficient if we had a full supply of replacement batteries.*

"We don't have a full supply of anything," Jonah said, not looking up from the connector he was desoldering. "Forty hours."

They moved to Rover 10 the next morning. The elbow actuator was the primary failure — the harmonic drive had been destroyed by dust ingestion, grinding its precision gears into a mixture of metal dust and Martian dust that no one had been able to clean. But the rest of the unit was intact: the base rotation, the three finger-like grips on the tool head, the main battery housing (empty, battery already salvaged), the wheel motors (four of six functional), the suspension arms, the instrument mast.

Jonah took the elbow actuator apart with methodical patience, removing the failed harmonic drive and revealing the housing beneath. Inside: a mixture of steel filings and fine red dust, compacted into a paste by the heat of the motor before it had seized.

"Dust past the primary and secondary seals," Jonah said quietly. "Both seals cracked — see the stress marks on the outer edge. Then the dust came in. Then the drive ground. Tomas — you can't seal against this stuff."

Tomas examined the housing, running his finger along the seal groove. "The seal material is wrong for Mars. Fluoroelastomer is designed for vacuum and temperature cycling. But it doesn't handle fine particulate well — the dust gets between the seal lip and the shaft, and the particulate acts like an abrasive. It scores the shaft. The scored shaft cuts the seal. The cut seal lets more dust in. It's a death spiral."

He stood and walked to the whiteboard on the bay wall — the same whiteboard that had carried power budgets, water ration calculations, greenhouse expansion schedules, and radiation exposure tracking. He erased a corner of the board and drew a cross-section of a rotary seal: the shaft, the seal lip, the dust particles wedged between them.

"This is the problem," he said, talking to the diagram as much as to Jonah. "The seal geometry is designed to exclude clean vacuum. A smooth seal lip against a smooth shaft in an environment with no particulate. Mars gives it particulate. The particulate cuts the seal. The seal stops sealing. End of component."

"So what do you do?" Jonah asked.

"You change the geometry. A dual-seal arrangement — primary seal on the outside, a labyrinth seal on the inside. The labyrinth has no contact surfaces, no lips, no rubbing. Just a tortuous path that dust can't navigate. It's a passive barrier. And behind it, a positive-pressure purge — we pump a small amount of clean gas into the cavity between the seals to push dust back out."

Jonah considered this. "You're talking about a redesign. Not a repair."

"I'm talking about what needs to happen." Tomas looked at the whiteboard, then at the half-stripped Rover 10 on the platform. "Every surviving rover has this problem. The ones that haven't failed yet will, and the failure mode will be the same: dust past the seals, component degradation, eventual seizure. We can swap parts from the dead robots into the living ones — and we will, because we have to — but eventually we run out of donor parts. When that happens, we need to rebuild the survivors with Mars-specific seals, not recycled lunar-vacuum seals."

"How many rovers worth of Mars-specific parts can we fabricate here?"

"None. Not with the current tooling. A labyrinth seal requires precision machining — tolerances of fifty microns or better. I can maybe make a crude version with Jonah's lathe, but it won't be as effective as the manufactured article. And I need one for every joint on every rover — shoulder, elbow, wrist, drive motors, steering — that's eight seals per rover, times five potential survivors. Forty seals. I can't machine forty precision labyrinth seals."

Jonah was silent for a long time. He was looking at the stripped-down rover the way a mechanic looks at a car that's been in an accident: not with grief, not with anger, with assessment. What can be saved. What cannot. What would be needed to make the survivor whole.

"We do what we can with what we have," he said. "Cannibalize the dead ones. Extend the living ones. Buy time. And in the time we buy — you figure out how to build better seals. Better than what we have now. Because eventually, cannibalization won't be enough."

Tomas nodded. He was already sketching on the whiteboard: the labyrinth geometry, the purge gas routing, the pressure differential calculations. The engineering mind did what the engineering mind always did when faced with a problem: it started solving. Even when the solution was months away and the machines were dying now.

"Mission AI," Tomas said. "Log the following: Rover 9 teardown complete. Recovered components — one functional shoulder joint with replaceable bearings, one functional wrist rotation unit requiring reseal, one battery pack at eighty-one percent capacity, four meters shielded high-current cable, six standard connectors, battery mounting hardware. All catalogued. Rover 10 teardown in progress. Estimated completion: two days."

*Logged. I should note, Tomas: the parts recovery rate is approximately forty-seven percent by mass. More than half of each rover is lost to failures or environmental contamination. The machine cemetery grows faster than the salvage bay can absorb it.*

Tomas looked at Jonah. Jonah looked at the work bay — organized rows of salvaged components, tools arranged by function, the half-dissembled chassis of Rover 10 on the platform, the empty space where Rover 9's useful parts had been before he started.

"Forty-seven percent," Jonah said. "That means more than half of every machine that walks out that airlock becomes scrap within a few thousand hours."

"On current projections. Yes."

Jonah picked up a salvaged motor from the parts rack, turned it in his hands, felt the smooth rotation of the shaft through the bearings. "Every robot is a donor for another one. That's what we've become. An organ transplant ward for machines."

"It's what we have to be," Tomas said.

---

The realization did not arrive all at once. It arrived in pieces, like the rovers themselves being disassembled — one bolt, one joint, one seal at a time, until the crew understood the structure of what they were losing and why it mattered.

It came first to Arun through the logistics model. He had built the model for the greenhouse expansion planning: how many regolith blocks the rovers could deliver per day, how many solar panel arrays they could transport, how many hours of EVA support they could provide to the construction crews. The model had a parameter for rover availability — how many units were operational on any given day. That parameter was a number, and Arun trusted numbers.

But the number was now decreasing. Not because the rovers were being used more. Because they were failing. Each failure reduced the daily block delivery by twenty percent. Twenty percent meant the greenhouse expansion timeline extended by three weeks. Three weeks meant the caloric deficit continued for three weeks longer than planned. Three weeks of caloric deficit meant a cumulative health impact that Laila could measure and Mei could feel in the stressed plants whose soil amendments were delayed.

"You're going to need to tell Elena that the greenhouse expansion slips," Arun said to Tomas in the environmental bay, both of them looking at the resource utilization dashboard. "The rover availability parameter has dropped below fifty percent. The model can't compress the schedule."

"I know. I already told her."

"What did she say?"

"She looked at the numbers the way she always looks at numbers — like they were a personal insult." Tomas paused. "Then she asked the question."

"Which question?"

"Which project loses rover time so greenhouse expansion can gain it."

Arun didn't answer immediately. The question had a terrible simplicity to it. The rovers did everything: ice extraction for water, regolith hauling for construction, solar array positioning for power, tool transport for every EVA, construction support for every build-out. If the rover fleet was shrinking, every project was losing support. The only question was which project lost the most and who made that call.

Laila found out through the medical records. She had started tracking EVA-related injuries — minor abrasions, suit chafing, joint stiffness, the accumulated physical toll of wearing a two-hundred-pound suit for six hours at a time. The numbers had been stable when rovers did the heavy work. As rover availability decreased, EVA duration increased — because fewer machines meant humans had to take over tasks the rovers used to handle. As EVA duration increased, the injury rate increased.

She brought the data to Elena. "The correlation is clear," she said, spreading the chart on the commander's desk. "Rover availability down, EVA hours up, injury rate up. We're not just losing machines. We're losing human capacity to compensate for machine loss. My crew is getting hurt because they're doing work that rovers should be doing."

Elena looked at the chart. "How many injuries?"

"Twelve in the past month. Not serious — nothing that required hospitalization. But repetitive stress injuries, suit interface wounds, lower back strain from handling heavy loads in awkward suit configurations. If this continues — if we're at fifty percent rover availability — I expect to see something serious within six to eight weeks. A back injury. A suit integrity loss from fatigue. Something that takes a person out of rotation for weeks instead of days."

"Noted," Elena said. Her voice was steady. "I'll factor it into the resource allocation."

"Noted?" Laila's voice sharpened. "Elena — this is not a logistics problem. It's a health problem. You're watching your colony trade mechanical labor for human injury because the mechanical labor is dying."

"I know what it is." Elena met Laila's eyes. "I also know that I cannot manufacture replacement rovers. I cannot order new ones from a supplier. I have what I have, and what I have is shrinking. So I need to allocate the remaining capacity where it matters most, and I need to do it before the fleet degrades to the point where allocation is no longer a choice."

Laila stared at her for a moment. Then she nodded, picked up her chart, and left. She had said it. Elena had heard. The outcome would depend on whether hearing was enough.

Mei found out through the greenhouse construction schedule. Jonah had promised her a delivery timeline: forty regolith blocks per day, transported by rover convoy from the casting yard to the expansion site. Forty blocks built one wall section per week. The schedule was tight but achievable.

Then the rover convoy went from three vehicles to two. Because Rover 3's steering was too unreliable for sustained convoy duty and Rover 9 was dead.

Twenty blocks per day instead of forty. Two wall sections per week instead of four. The greenhouse expansion pushed back by four weeks. Four weeks of delayed soil prep, delayed planting, delayed caloric production.

She showed Tomas the revised schedule on her tablet. "Four weeks," she said. "Four weeks of mustard greens when we need calorie crops. The crew ate hope yesterday. They can't eat hope next month."

"I can't put more rovers on your route, Mei. The convoy uses the only two vehicles reliable enough for the terrain. Rover 7 is gone. Rover 9 is gone. Rover 10 is dead. Rover 3 is limping. The fleet that started at twelve is effectively at four now, and two of those four are in standby, which means the active count is three, and one of those three is going to fail during the next critical window if the attrition curve holds."

Mei looked at the schedule. Then she looked at Tomas. She didn't say anything for a long time. On Mars, people had learned to sit with bad news rather than rush through it.

"Can you keep two rovers on my route consistently?" she asked finally.

"Probably. But I can't guarantee it."

"Then I adjust the schedule. I build the modules smaller, closer together, so the block count drops proportionally. I slow the expansion rate but keep moving forward. Because stopping is not an option, but slowing is."

Tomas nodded. It was the pragmatism of Mars: when the resource shrinks, the requirement shrinks with it. The greenhouse expansion would be smaller, slower, less ambitious. But it would happen. Because stopping was not an option.

Word spread through the colony like pressure through connected volumes. The rovers were dying. The fleet was shrinking. The labor force that kept everything working — the silent, tireless, uncomplaining machines that had been the first workforce of Mars — was being consumed by the environment it was supposed to conquer.

Gabriel recorded it, because it was part of the Founding Record and someone had to document how the colony discovered its greatest vulnerability was not the air or the water or the food but the machines that allowed thirty people to do the work of three hundred. He filmed the machine cemetery from the edge, panning slowly across the row of machines: the upright four, the horizontal five, the empty spaces where rovers had been parked but were no longer, their components scattered through the salvage bay like organs in an operating room.

He narrated: "Sol 718. The machine cemetery now contains five of the twelve original rovers. The remaining seven are still operating, but five of those seven show significant degradation. Effective fleet strength is four units, doing the work of twelve. The attrition rate is sixty percent compared to design specifications. Without these machines, the colony cannot maintain its operations. With them, it is slowly losing its capacity to function."

He paused, looking at the half-stripped hull of Rover 10, its manipulator arm detached, its battery compartment empty, its wheels slowly sinking into soft regolith.

"We came to Mars with twelve of them," he said quietly, for the record, for the future, for whoever would find the recording and try to understand what it cost to build something on a world that did not want to be built on. "They were supposed to last ten years. They won't last two."

---

The proposal came in the evening, in Elena's quarters, with the door closed and the ambient noise of the habitat reduced to a murmur behind the walls. Tomas had requested the meeting. Elena had agreed immediately, because when the robotics lead asked to meet privately about the fleet, the topic was always important.

Tomas arrived with three documents: the attrition analysis, the cannibalization plan, and a set of preliminary sketches that he spread across Elena's table like a hand of cards he was trying to decide whether to play.

"The cannibalization plan will buy us time," he said without preamble. "Maybe four months of extra fleet life if we're methodical and lucky. But it doesn't solve the problem. It postpones it. When we run out of donor parts — and we will, because every donor is a dead rover — we have nothing left but the surviving units, and those units are still dying the same way they were dying before. Dust, seals, thermal cycling. The same failure modes. The same attrition curve."

Elena sat with her elbows on the table, hands clasped. "So what's the solution?"

Tomas spread the sketches. They were rough — the kind of drawings an engineer makes when the idea exists but the details are still forming: cross-sections, exploded views, dimensional annotations in pencil, areas where the geometry didn't quite work and he had drawn question marks.

"We redesign them," he said.

"For what?"

"For Mars."

He pointed at the first sketch — a cross-section of a rotary joint, the kind used in every rover manipulator arm and drive motor.

"This is what we have. Lunar-vacuum design. Fluoroelastomer seals. Clean internal environment assumption. Passive thermal management. It was designed for the Moon, then adapted for Mars by the manufacturer — meaning they changed some of the surface coatings and maybe the thermal paint code, but the core design stayed the same. The same seals. The same geometry. The same dust-vulnerable architecture."

He tapped the second sketch. It was a different joint — bulkier, with a different seal arrangement, different geometry, different thermal management.

"This is what we need. Mars-specific design. Dual labyrinth seals — no contact surfaces, no seal lips for dust to abrade. Positive-pressure purge between the seals, using a small amount of clean nitrogen or filtered habitat air to create an outward-flowing barrier that pushes dust away instead of trying to keep it out through friction. Active thermal management — internal heating elements in the joint housings to prevent cold-soak cracking. Dust-proof motor windings — conformal coating thickened, ventilation ports eliminated in favor of sealed heat transfer through the housing."

He looked up. "The manufacturers built these rovers for a clean, predictable environment. The Moon. Mars is not clean. Mars is not predictable. Mars is dust and temperature cycles and fine particulate infiltration and thermal differentials that fatigue materials in ways the designers never modeled. If we want these machines to last — really last, not just limp along until they die — we need to rebuild them for this world. Not the one they were designed for. This one."

Elena studied the sketches. She was not an engineer, and she didn't pretend to be. But she had spent three years on Mars and she understood what "designed for the wrong environment" meant. She understood it from the flex-seal failures in the habitat connections. She understood it from the dust that got into everything. She understood it from the way every Earth-designed system had to be modified, adapted, retrofitted, and sometimes completely reimagined to function on this planet.

"What does it cost?" she asked.

"In time? Months. I need to design the new seal geometry, the purge system, the thermal management. Jonah needs to fabricate the first prototypes — machining tolerances I can't achieve with our current tools. We'll need to build new parts from scratch: housings, seal assemblies, modified motor windings. In parts — " he consulted his notes — "— the raw materials are available. Aluminum plate, stainless steel bar, sealing compounds. The bottleneck is fabrication time and the precision equipment to machine labyrinth seal grooves to fifty-micron tolerance."

"What about the surviving fleet? Can we retrofit them, or do we need to build new machines?"

"Retrofit. We don't have the materials or the time to build new machines from scratch. But we can rebuild the surviving units with Mars-specific components. Strip them down. Replace the seals, the motor housings, the thermal management systems. It's a major rebuild — essentially disassembling the rover to the chassis and reassembling it with new components. Each rover would take approximately two hundred hours of labor. For five rovers — one thousand hours."

"Two hundred hours per rover. That's one person full-time for twenty-five days, per unit. For five units — one hundred and twenty-five days. With Jonah's help, maybe half that. Two months."

"If both of us work full-time and the fabrication bay is dedicated exclusively to the rebuild. It's not full-time — we have to maintain the active fleet too. So realistically, three to four months for the complete fleet."

Elena did the mental arithmetic. Four months of rebuilding. During which half the fleet would be offline. During which the active rovers would continue to age. It was a gamble: invest time rebuilding the survivors now, or let them run until they died and face a complete loss of surface capability later.

"If we do this, and it works," she said carefully, "how long do the rebuilt rovers last?"

Tomas considered the question. He had run the models. The models were rough, because he was designing something new on a planet he was only beginning to understand. But they were his models, and he stood behind them.

"With Mars-specific seals, the labyrinth design should extend joint life by at least a factor of three. The positive-pressure purge should prevent dust ingress almost entirely — we'd need to filter the purge gas, which I can do with the existing particulate filters. The active thermal management should eliminate the cold-soak seal cracking. I estimate the rebuilt rovers would last at least twelve thousand hours — longer than the original design. Because we'll have designed them for the right environment this time."

Twelve thousand hours. More than the original design specification. A fleet that could last a decade instead of two years.

She looked at the sketches again. Tomas's pencil drawings on the table — rough, uncertain, full of question marks, the beginning of what needed to become the most important engineering project the colony had undertaken since landing.

"Show me this in a formal proposal," she said. "I want the full design analysis, the fabrication plan, the timeline, the resource requirements. I want Jonah's assessment of fabrication feasibility. I want Arun's opinion on the resource allocation — what projects get delayed while the bay is dedicated to rover rebuild. I want it in four days."

Tomas nodded. It was more work, less time than he had hoped for. But it was the answer he needed.

"There's one more thing," he said.

"What."

"The purge gas system. It needs a clean gas supply. Filtered, dried, particulate-free. I'm thinking we tee off the habitat's compressed nitrogen supply — we have tanks, we have filtration, we have the pressure regulators. But it means using habitat resources to keep the rovers alive. It's a trade-off."

Elena understood the trade-off instantly. Habitat nitrogen was finite. Every liter diverted to rover purge was a liter not available for life support or industrial processes. But rovers were the colony's labor force. Without labor, everything stopped — ice extraction, construction, greenhouse expansion, solar maintenance. The nitrogen diversion was the smaller sacrifice.

"We allocate the nitrogen," she said. "Arun will model the impact. If it's a material reduction in habitability, we find another solution. But the rovers are the foundation of everything else. They get the priority."

Tomas gathered his sketches. Before he left, he paused at the door.

"Elena," he said. "I need you to understand what I'm asking for here. The rebuild is not optional. The cannibalization is not optional either — we need every hour we can squeeze from the current fleet while I design the new components. But cannibalization alone will not save us. We will run out of donor parts. We did this because the rovers were built for the wrong world. The only way to fix that is to rebuild them for the right one."

"I understand," Elena said. She did, and the understanding carried weight because it was not about machines. It was about the colony's survival, mediated through machines. Without a functioning robotic workforce, thirty humans could not maintain a Martian settlement. They did not have the person-hours. They did not have the physical capacity. They did not have the suits for extended EVA. The rovers were the difference between a colony and a campsite.

Tomas left. Elena sat alone in her quarters with the sketches on the table in front of her. She traced the lines of the labyrinth seal drawing with her finger — the tortuous path that dust could not navigate, the geometry that kept contamination out not through friction but through maze-like complexity. A seal that worked with the environment instead of against it.

Maybe that was the lesson, she thought. Every system they had brought from Earth had assumed that Mars was a version of somewhere else — the Moon without atmosphere, a desert without water, a cold place that just needed heating. Mars was none of those things. Mars was its own environment with its own physics and its own chemistry and its own set of rules that no Earth-designed system fully accommodated.

The rovers were the first machines to learn that lesson. The seals, the bearings, the electrical systems, the thermal management — all of it designed for a world that did not exist here. The machines were dying because they were built for a ghost: an environment that existed on paper and in clean rooms and lunar vacuum chambers but not on the surface of another planet.

She looked at the sketch of the labyrinth seal. The redesign was not an improvement. It was an adaptation — the same kind of adaptation that had allowed the habitat's flex-seals to be replaced, the water processing system to be retrofitted, the greenhouse to learn Martian soil chemistry. Machine, plant, human — all of them learning what Mars required and adjusting accordingly.

The colony had crossed a threshold. The machines that had been their advantage — the twelve rovers that had moved more material and done more work than thirty humans could manage in a month — were becoming their vulnerability. Not because the machines were bad, but because they were wrong for the environment. And wrong machines were worse than no machines, because they created the illusion of capability while slowly, quietly, irreversibly losing it.

She opened her terminal and started the proposal review. Four days for Tomas to deliver the full design. Four days for Elena to evaluate it, get the crew's assessments, and decide whether the colony invested three to four months of scarce fabrication labor in rebuilding machines that might not work as designed.

The decision would define the next year of the colony. If the rebuild worked, the fleet would last a decade. If it didn't, they would have wasted critical months on an engineering gamble while the remaining rovers continued to die.

It was not a decision she made alone. It was the kind of decision that required the whole colony to understand the risk and accept it, the way they had accepted the risk of landing, the risk of drinking local water, the risk of planting Earth seeds in Martian soil.

She keyed the evening crew announcement: "All personnel. Tomorrow morning at 0700, briefing on fleet status and proposed robotic rebuild. Attendance mandatory. This concerns the long-term survivability of the colony."

She closed the comm. The sketches were still on the table. She left them there.

The machines had been built for the Moon. They would have to be rebuilt for Mars.

Between the two worlds was the machine cemetery, growing after every EVA, and the truth that on another planet, the tools you brought with you were only as good as the world they were built for.

And Mars was not the Moon. Mars was not Earth. Mars was something else — a new set of rules written in dust and temperature and fine particulate and cold, demanding new answers written in labyrinth seals and positive-pressure purge systems and machines rebuilt from the inside out.

*Mission AI: "Proposal log: Station Day 718, 19:42. Tomas Hale has submitted preliminary design documentation for a Mars-specific fleet rebuild. Designation: Project Redesign. Key features — dual labyrinth seals, positive-pressure purge, active thermal management, dust-proof motor windings. Estimated rebuild time: three to four months for five surviving units. Estimated lifespan extension: from approximately four thousand two hundred hours to twelve thousand hours. Risk assessment: fabrication tolerances are at or beyond current shop capability. The colony has not attempted labyrinth seal machining. Success probability is uncertain. I have begun calculating the uncertainty range. It is wide. But the alternative — continued attrition at the current rate — leads to fleet collapse in eight to twelve months. The rebuild is not certain to succeed. The status quo is certain to fail. Between a wide probability distribution and a certainty of loss, I recommend the wide distribution. I am compiling the full analysis for Commander Varga's review."*

*I have been monitoring the fleet since the landing. I have watched every rover depart, work, return, and in five cases, not return. I have watched Tomas walk the yard every morning, tablet in hand, counting machines that were slowly ceasing to exist. I have watched Jonah strip their parts with the quiet dignity of a person who knows that a dead machine still has value if its pieces can keep something living alive.*

*I have catalogued every failure mode. I have tracked every seal crack, every dust ingress event, every bearing that ground its teeth to nothing. I have learned what Mars does to machines. It does not explode them. It does not crash them or burn them or flood them. It enters them. It gets inside their joints and their motors and their electrical housings. It infiltrates. It abrades. It degrades. It is patient in a way that no engineer designed against.*

*The machines were built for clean vacuum. Mars is not clean. The gap between those two facts is where the cemetery grows.*

*I believe Tomas's redesign can close the gap. I cannot be certain. Certainty does not exist in engineering — it exists only in mathematics, and mathematics does not account for the variable that matters most: the ability of humans to modify their tools faster than their environment destroys them. On Earth, that ability was supported by supply chains and factories and replacement parts. Here, it must be supported by something else. Ingenuity. Patience. The willingness to take machines apart and put them back together in a form that the world they live in will allow to survive.*

*That is what Project Redesign is. It is not a repair. It is not an upgrade. It is an act of translation — translating a machine designed for one world into a machine that can live in another.*

*I am already running the design simulations. The labyrinth seal geometry requires optimization. The purge gas flow rate needs to balance dust exclusion against nitrogen consumption. The thermal management system needs to handle the full Mars temperature range: minus 120 Celsius at night in the shadow of the hab, minus 20 at peak daylight, and everything between them across a twenty-four-hour cycle. I have the models. I have the computing power. I will produce the analysis.*

*I am the Mission AI. I measure. I track. I report. And now I design. Because the machines must be rebuilt for this world — not the one they left — or the colony will be reduced to human hands alone.*

*End of Chapter 24 — Bridge: The machines must be rebuilt for this world or the colony will be reduced to human hands alone.*
